Should your small business website be in Hindi, English or both?

A hypothetical Varanasi printing shop uses a quote request to decide which pages and steps to offer in Hindi.

By SiteSutra · 25 November 2026

← All articlesYour next step ↓

Start with the language your customers can use to complete the task that matters most. Add a second language when it helps a distinct group finish that task and someone on your team can keep both versions accurate. For a small business, that might mean offering one complete enquiry journey in both languages before translating the rest of the site.

A print shop follows one quote request

Imagine Kavita runs a hypothetical printing shop in Varanasi. A school administrator ordering event banners needs to check turnaround, find out which artwork files the shop accepts and ask for a quote. Kavita can discuss all of this in Hindi, but the English website uses phrases like “print ready artwork” without explaining them. The quote form also assumes the customer has a file ready to attach.

She compares two proposals. One adds a Hindi version of every page, including a long portfolio. The other starts with the banner service page and the quote request it leads to. She traces the customer's route on a phone and notices that translating the service description alone would still leave the customer reading English field labels, errors and confirmation messages.

Decide how far the second language needs to go

Kavita’s choices for the banner enquiry journey
What the customer needsScope to considerWhat to check
Help with a few technical termsPlain English with a short explanation of artwork, file size and dimensionsAsk a buyer to explain what they need to send using their own words
Read terms and request a quote in HindiHindi service page with a usable Hindi contact routeAsk a reader to find the turnaround information, complete the request and explain what happens next
Compare several services and return laterExpand the language coverage to the journeys customers regularly useGive each translated page an owner who can update both versions when a service changes

Check recent enquiry conversations for the point where people ask for help. Pay attention to language and script separately. A customer who speaks Hindi might prefer reading it in Devanagari or might be more comfortable with an English label they already recognise. Let people try the actual copy on their phones, and ask where they hesitated. A small test helps improve the wording and scope.

Write the handoff and the recovery path

Kavita asks the colleague who answers quote requests to review the proposed Hindi copy. They agree on the details that let the shop reply usefully: the finished banner dimensions, the intended date and whether the customer already has artwork. They make the upload optional and explain what to do if the file is too large.

When a field is missing, the error should tell the reader how to continue in the same language as the form. The confirmation should say how the shop will reply. If a button opens WhatsApp, tell the visitor they still need to send the message there. Check the first staff reply too. A Hindi enquiry route works best when the team can respond in Hindi.

Give each translated page an address people can share

If the English and Hindi versions are public web pages, give each a stable URL and link directly between equivalent versions. Place the language choice where someone arriving from a shared link can find it. Google recommends separate URLs, visible links between versions and avoiding automatic language redirects that could prevent people and crawlers from reaching a page. Ask the developer to use hreflang for equivalent language versions. Google Search Central guidance for multilingual websites.

Set the HTML document language to match the page, such as lang="hi" for the Hindi version. This gives assistive technologies a language cue for pronunciation. On a phone, read the Devanagari text at a larger text size and check that characters render clearly and form labels, errors and buttons still fit. W3C guidance on identifying a page’s language.

Agree who updates both versions

At the shop, turnaround depends on the material and whether the artwork is ready. Kavita keeps those conditions in one shared reference and assigns one staff member to check both pages, the form and the confirmation when the process changes. She also checks where each language link leads when a translation is unavailable. A customer should be able to tell before following a link that the destination is in English.

Use the website language journey worksheet (CSV) to record one customer task, the point where language creates friction, the pages or messages to revise and the people who will review them. Keep the notes about the task and omit customer names or message transcripts.

Test one request from start to finish

Kavita starts with the banner enquiry because it has a named reviewer and a clear end point. She asks a Hindi reader to find the artwork requirements, request a quote without a file and explain how the shop will respond. The team uses that observation to decide what to revise and which service, if any, to translate next.

For a wider redesign, use the website project brief to record language ownership and the enquiry form test guide to verify receipt. SiteSutra’s website development service explains how to scope the build.
